passage: I'm Leela, Harsha's cousin, and I stayed at their house during the holidays. Before dinner, Harsha dragged his little stool to the sink on his own, rubbed the soap into bubbles and held his wet hands up for the towel, grinning. But at bedtime, when his mother brought his pyjamas, he threw himself on the floor, kicking and yelling "No!" I couldn't tell if he was tired or just wanted to keep playing. Maybe both.

qa.q: What did Harsha drag to the sink before dinner?
qa.a: He dragged his little stool to the sink on his own.

qa.q: How can you tell Harsha felt proud of washing his hands?
qa.a: He held his wet hands up for the towel, grinning, which suggests he liked doing the routine himself.

qa.q: What could help Harsha's bedtime go more smoothly?
qa.a: His mother could give a gentle warning before bedtime and let him choose between two pyjamas, keeping the same calm steps each night.

qa.q: Why might Leela be unsure about the reason for Harsha's tantrum?
qa.a: Leela only sees what he does from the outside, so Leela can guess tiredness or wanting to play but can't know which it was.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a handwashing routine but resisting bedtime with a tantrum, seen by a cousin.

passage:
Tuesday: When Nirmala started the tidy-up song, Ojas flung a block across the room and lay face down on the rug, howling.
Friday: She sang again and dropped one car into the basket. Ojas watched, then put in two cars himself before wandering off.
The next Thursday: Hearing the first line of the song, Ojas began carrying blocks to the basket, humming along, and looked up at Nirmala after each one.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do on Friday while singing?
qa.a: She sang again and dropped one car into the basket.

qa.q: What does Ojas looking up at Nirmala after each block suggest he wanted?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted her to notice and share his pleasure in helping tidy up.

qa.q: Why did the tidy-up song help Ojas learn the routine?
qa.a: The same song each time signalled what was coming, and Nirmala tidying with him made it feel like a shared game rather than an order. 🎉

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt on the first Tuesday?
qa.a: She may have felt tired or frustrated by the howling, yet she kept the song going on later days.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from resisting a toy-pickup routine with a tantrum to joining it over time.

passage: It was brushing time in their small Pune flat. Uma, two and a half, clamped her mouth shut and turned her face into the pillow when Alka held out the toothbrush. Alka didn't argue. She handed Uma her cloth doll and a second brush. "Can you brush Guddi's teeth?" Uma scrubbed the doll's face hard, giggling. Then she opened her own mouth wide, and Alka brushed quickly while Uma watched Guddi.

qa.q: What did Alka hand Uma along with the second brush?
qa.a: She handed Uma her cloth doll.

qa.q: Why might Uma have clamped her mouth shut at first?
qa.a: She may have felt tired or wanted some control over her own body, so she resisted the routine.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Alka, and why?
qa.a: Letting Uma brush the doll first turned the routine into play and gave her some control, so she opened her mouth willingly.

qa.q: What would change if Alka had forced the brush into Uma's mouth?
qa.a: Brushing might become a nightly fight, and Uma could start dreading bedtime.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler resisting a bedtime routine and then joining it through play.

passage:
"Yamini, bath time's over. Teeth now."
"No teeth!" Yamini flung the brush on the floor and flopped down.
"Hmm." Harsha sat beside her. "Who brushes first, you or Teddy?"
She peeked. "Teddy."
Harsha brushed the bear's fuzzy mouth. "Your turn."
"Me do!" She grabbed the brush and chewed it, grinning.
"Good job. Then story, then sleep."
"Two story!"
"One story, Yamini."

qa.q: Who brushed first before Yamini?
qa.a: Teddy, her bear, got brushed first.

qa.q: Why did Yamini fling the brush and flop down?
qa.a: She did not want to stop playing and resisted the routine, feeling frustrated at being told what to do.

qa.q: Which choice by Harsha worked, and why?
qa.a: Turning brushing into a game with Teddy let Yamini feel in charge, so she joined in instead of fighting.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had shouted and forced the brush in?
qa.a: Bedtime might have become a battle, and Yamini could start dreading the routine instead of slowly accepting it.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler moving between resisting and accepting a bedtime hygiene routine.

passage:
Weekly crèche note, by Ganga Didi
Omkar is learning 'tidy-up time'. On Monday he threw himself down and kicked when the bell rang. On Wednesday he put two cars in the basket after I sang our clean-up song. Today he carried the whole basket to the shelf himself and looked at me, chest out. 🙂 He still cries when it's time to wash hands, so we are working on that next.

qa.q: What did Omkar do on Monday when the bell rang?
qa.a: He threw himself down and kicked.

qa.q: What does Omkar looking at Ganga Didi with his chest out suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud of carrying the basket and wanted her to notice.

qa.q: How could Ganga Didi use what worked for tidy-up with handwashing?
qa.a: She could add a short song or a fun step to handwashing too, since the song helped tidy-up become a routine.

qa.q: How might Omkar's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel encouraged by his progress and understanding about the handwashing crying, since it shows he is still learning.

grounding: Shows a toddler slowly adopting a toy-pickup routine while still resisting handwashing.
